- A fault ends that pack's tour, because the next frame boundary past a bad head is unknown. A pack therefore reports at most one fault.
- A required kind that the opener does not support is reported as `Kind(k)`.
- Any other failure ends the step with that `Error`: `Io`, or `Full(Allocation(c))`.

**Not checked, and why (reversible):**
- Page body decode and the order of outgoing edges. Open checks them. A reachable frame whose bytes match its parent's pointer is the frame our writer placed there, and §2.8's host rule forbids guarding against our own writer.
- The MANIFEST and journal segments. Open rereads them whole.

A later version may add these, and a periodic tour with an I/O budget, without a format change.

**Laws** (`store-scrub.hirsel`):
- **Misdirected write, seen from both sides.** In TigerBeetle's fault model, pack A's first frame lands at offset 72 of pack B, and A's slot keeps its old sector (zeros). A tour over the damaged generation reports exactly (A, 72, `Kind(0)`) and (B, 72, `Checksum`). B's frame has a well-formed head, but its check binds A's sequence. The Db still answers reads.
- **Stale frame at its own place.** A frame resealed for pack C at 72, with its last byte changed, gives (C, 72, `Checksum`), from the pointer check alone.
- **Clean control.** Before the damage, the same generation reads with no fault, and `checked` equals the sum of the listed packs' file sizes.
- **A scrub racing compaction.** A tour is begun, then a cut retires every data pack it holds. Each held file still exists, and the tour finishes clean. After the tour is dropped, the next cut leaves exactly the still-listed packs on disk.

### 11.18 Bucket authority (v2.43, deleted by v2.46)

Replaced by §12's objects@1. There is no reader for a v2.43 bucket store.

### 11.19 Read-only open (v2.44, deleted by v2.46)

Replaced by §12.5's `Follower`: `open_read_only`, `open_bucket_read_only`, `ReadOnly`, `read_only_table`, `read_only_get` and `read_only_version` are deleted. A follower over log@1 is the old offline reader, under writer exclusion, reading the last segment past END as §3.4 does (§12.5). Its S2 `read-only` crash law is kept, restated over a follower (§12.10).

**Callers that move with it (v2.47, Fable L6).** The deleted API has five callers outside the store's implementation. Each moves to a log@1 `follower` under writer exclusion, or to the writer's own Db, in the slice that deletes the API:

| Caller | Uses | Moves to |
|---|---|---|
| `core/programs/platform/local.hirsel` | 2 | a follower over the place's directory |
| `core/programs/platform/platform.hirsel` | 3 | a follower over the place's directory |
| `core/programs/harness/gateway_laws.hirsel` | 1 | a follower in the law |
| `core/programs/harness/waits.hirsel` | 2 | a follower, `catch_up` with a deadline |
| `core/std/api/store.md` | 2 | the follower API's text |

The implementation's own uses (`store.hirsel`, `store-bucket.hirsel`, `bucket_laws.hirsel`) are deleted with the API.

## 12. Authorities, the claim fence, levels and followers (Store M2, v2.49, not yet built)

Background, design history and prior art: `/workspace/code/hirsel-briefs/store-m2-spec-1919/DESIGN.md` (v2.45). Where DESIGN and this section differ, this section is the contract. v2.46 applied Sam's rulings Q1–Q5 of 2026-11-23. v2.47 fixes the two blind re-checks of v2.46 (`m2-recheck-astra-1932`, `m2-recheck-fable-1933`). v2.48 fixes the v2.47 delta check (`m2-delta-astra-1948`, cited "Delta #n"). v2.49 fixes the v2.48 delta check (`m2-v248-astra-1950`, cited "Check #n"). Q1–Q5 stand unchanged. See CHANGES-v2.49, CHANGES-v2.48 and CHANGES-v2.47.

**Citations.** In this section "Astra #n" can name the v2.46 attack (m2-attack-1924, its An) or the v2.47 re-check (m2-recheck-astra-1932, its #n), and "Fable Fn" the v2.46 review while "Fable L/S/A n" the re-check. CHANGES-v2.47's table is the authoritative map from each re-check finding to its rule, and CHANGES-v2.46's from each earlier finding.

**One rule about clocks.** No *safety* rule reads a clock. Fencing, freshness, staleness, reclaim and the claim are decided by positions, epochs and register bytes. Two *liveness* rules use the local monotonic clock only:
- request deadlines (`op_ms`, `deadline_ns`, `claim_ms`);
- the idle head poll (§12.3).

Neither compares clocks across machines.

### 12.1 The authority

An authority keeps a store's history. Each store has exactly one, fixed at genesis and recorded in HEADER `authority`: 0 log, 1 objects, 2 sim. A memory store writes no file. The program receives the authority as a value made from a grant:

```hirsel
pub fn memory_authority() -> Authority                                                        // authority.memory@1
pub fn log_authority(d: Dir) -> Authority                                                    // authority.log@1
pub fn object_authority(take c: std.object.Client, level: String, op_ms: u64) -> Authority   // authority.objects@1
pub fn sim_authority(take c: std.object.Client, levels: SimLevels, take sync: LevelSync, op_ms: u64) -> Authority   // authority.sim@1 (v2.73)
```

**sim@1's grant (v2.73).** sim@1 is objects@1's protocol over a `std.sim.s3` client (§12.2, §12.4). The level declaration and the weak barriers are the only additions:

```hirsel
pub type SimLevels: send { weak: List[String], strongest: String }   // weakest first; each weak level survives 0, the strongest 2
pub opaque type LevelWorld                  // a law's weak barriers and their ground-truth log
pub opaque type LevelSync: send             // one open's endpoint to its LevelWorld
pub type LevelUntil: send = Never | At(u64) | AfterSynced(String, u64)   // sim-clock ns; another level's synced position
pub type LevelHold: send { level: String, until: LevelUntil }
pub type LevelKind: send = Requested(u64) | Synced(u64) | Mark(u64)            // a position, or the law's label
pub type LevelEvent: send { level: String, epoch: u64, kind: LevelKind, at_ns: u64 }
pub fn level_world(tasks: Tasks, clock: Clock, take holds: List[LevelHold], world_bytes: u64) -> Result[LevelWorld, Error] waits   // clock: the sim's
pub fn level_sync(mut w: LevelWorld) -> Result[LevelSync, Error]                // one per open, and one per law that marks
pub fn level_mark(mut s: LevelSync, label: u64) -> Result[(), Error] waits      // logs Mark(label) at the sim clock's now
pub fn level_log(take w: LevelWorld) -> Result[List[LevelEvent], Error] waits   // ends the world and returns its log in order
```

The creating task owns `LevelWorld` because it holds the CONC-1 task handle. Dropping that handle before `level_log` joins it cancels the world. Opens receive the sendable `LevelSync` endpoint.

The register is the `std.sim.s3` service the law starts once (`start_service`). Each open gets a client made from that service's `Endpoint`, so two opens, two holders or a crash and a claim all reach one register. The service's `Plan` schedules faults for every client of the service. A `Plan` holds no register and no declaration. Holds are declared when the world starts and released by their `until`, so no task has to be free to release one. A held level completes no barrier until its `until` is met, and then completes the latest requested position of each open. `at_ns` reads the sim's clock, the same clock that stamps `std.sim.s3`'s request log, so a law can order the two logs.

**The selection.** Every writer open names what it expects to find. A launch's selection is a value of these three `Options` fields:
- `o.expect: Option[StoreId]`;
- `o.activation: Option[u64]`;
- `o.binding: Option[Digest]` (v2.55; `o.binding` before), the 32-byte digest (AM8's `Digest`) that binds the store to a release: the runner's identity digest (RUNNER §6 "One identity", v2.42), which covers the release's code, allowance and exported list and not its executable bytes. The runner computes it. The store treats it as opaque bytes and only compares them.

HEAD records the store identity (in its HEADER), the current `activation` and the current activation's `binding` (§12.2). Each is set at genesis and changed only by the head write of an activation CHECKPOINT (§12.7). This applies Astra #5 (v2.47).

**Opening checks, all made before any write (Q4, Astra #5, #11, #13, #21).** They run on the observed head. With no head, they run before genesis's first create.
- An authority of another kind than the store's HEADER is `Unsupported(kind)`.
- If `o.expect = Some(id)`, a head of another identity is `Foreign`. **No head** with `o.expect = Some(_)` is `NotFound`, and genesis never runs. An existing deployment whose grant points at an empty namespace is refused; a new identity is never created in its place.
- An AUTHORITY frame naming another `bucket` or `prefix` than the live client is `Foreign`. The recorded endpoint may differ from the live one, and is never checked (§12.2).
- If the grant's level declaration differs from the recorded one (§12.4), the result is `Declared(name)`, naming the first recorded level that differs (v2.73: the recorded name, never the grant's).
- If `o.activation = Some(v)` and the head's `activation` ≠ v, the result is `NotCurrent(head.activation)`. No head with `o.activation = Some(v)` and v ≠ 0 is `NotFound`.
- If `o.binding = Some(d)`, the head's `activation` is at least 1 and its `binding` ≠ d, the result is `NotCurrent(head.activation)`. A head at activation 0 has no binding (genesis records all zeros), and no head has none, so the check does not apply to them: the runner's genesis install sets the first binding (§12.7, RUNNER §6). So any open whose launch binding is not the active one fails here, `Current(v)` and `Reopen` alike, before it can replace OLD's head. An explicit install (`Install`, RUNNER §6) passes `o.binding = None`: it is authorized to replace the active binding, and its install sets the new one.
- objects@1 only: if the live client fails §12.2's transport check ("Which endpoints the store accepts"), the result is `Endpoint(Insecure)` or `Endpoint(Unproven)`.
- sim@1 only (v2.73): a client that is not a `std.sim.s3` client is `Endpoint(NotSimulator)`. A `SimLevels` outside §12.2's AUTHORITY ranges (more than 15 weak names, or a name of 0 or over 64 bytes) is `Limit(Name)`, and a name given twice, the strongest included, is `Exists(name)`. Both are refused before any request.

None of these is retried by `open`'s claim loop, and none writes a byte.

**Open identity (§1.12, Astra #19, #22).**
- On log@1 an open's number is the first segment the open creates, as today.
- On objects@1 and sim@1 a writer open's number is its epoch. Each writer open claims, and epochs never repeat.
- A follower's number is `2⁶³ | n`, with n drawn from its process owner's **`Followers` source**, which keeps a counter that only rises. The process owner creates one source and reuses it for every follower. Snapshots, resume tokens and shared-view caches are process-local, so a number that cannot repeat within the process is enough. No random draw is involved. Epochs and segment numbers stay below 2⁶³: one that would reach 2⁶³ is `Limit(Ids)` before any write. So a follower's number never equals a writer's.

### 12.2 The history and its names

**log@1 is today's directory store, unchanged in format and GC** (§2–§11, format 3).
- Its history is the journal and the MANIFEST, and its fence is the OFD lock on LOCK.
- It writes no CLAIM. `retain`, `checkpoint_entries`, `claim_ms`, `head_poll_ms` and `binding` do not apply to it. On log@1 the runner keeps its post-open `Describe` comparison under LOCK, as built, and a probe refused there reads its deploy's witness before releasing LOCK (§12.7, v2.50).
- Its one level is `host`, which is today's `durable`. ENDSTATE's `process` level waits until §3.4 keeps valid frames above a segment's synced end.

The rest of this section is objects@1. sim@1 is the same protocol over a `std.sim.s3` client, with HEADER `authority` 2, its declaration in AUTHORITY and the level rule of §12.4 (v2.73). Its objects carry `epoch` exactly as objects@1's do.

**Every objects@1 object is a format-3 file (AP1).**
- Its HEADER carries `authority` 1 and its creating `epoch`, which is non-zero only on objects@1.
- Frame checks keep §2.1's 33-byte binding unchanged: `identity ‖ role ‖ seq ‖ offset`, with `seq` the HEADER's (a position, generation or pack seq). **The binding never contains an object name, so it is not circular** (Astra #1, Fable F8).
- An object's **digest** is xxh3-64 (seed 0) over its complete bytes, from offset 0 to its end, computed after every frame is sealed. The digest appears in the object's name and in whatever references it (LINK, HEAD, MARK, LOCATE). A reader recomputes it over the bytes it read, and a mismatch is `Corrupt(Fault{file: name, offset: 0, why: Checksum})`.
- A HEADER whose `role`, `seq` or `epoch` differs from the name's is `Corrupt(Header)`. So a copy moved to another position's or epoch's name fails before its digest is compared.

**Names.** All names sit under the AUTHORITY's `prefix`. Numbers are decimal, zero-padded to 20 digits, and digests are 16 lower-case hex digits.

| Key | Role | Bytes | Written by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `head` | 7 | HEADER(seq = position) ‖ HEAD ‖ AUTHORITY | genesis: create (`If-None-Match: *`); after that only `store_if` with `Match(t)` (§12.3) |
| `e-<position>-<epoch>-<digest>` | 2 | one entry: HEADER(seq = position, `prev_end` 0) ‖ LINK ‖ body frames | create-only |
| `m-<generation>-<epoch>-<digest>` | 1 | a MANIFEST (AP14) | create-only |
| `p-<seq>-<epoch>-<digest>` | 3 | a pack (class 0, 1 or 2) | create-only multipart (`upload(NoClobber)`, `parts`, `complete`) |
| `l-<position>-<epoch>-<digest>` | 8 | a locator chunk: HEADER(seq = the position of the CHECKPOINT entry that first wrote it) ‖ one LOCATE frame (v2.47, "The pack locator") | create-only |

- **Create-only everywhere** (Astra #20). Every entry, MANIFEST, pack and chunk is written with `If-None-Match: *`, and a name is never written twice with different bytes:
  - one holder writes an entry's (position, epoch) once. An epoch has one holder, and a holder that cannot finish an entry write is poisoned, so it never writes that position again;
  - a holder never reuses a pack seq or MANIFEST generation within its epoch, including numbers consumed by refused cuts. Its counters only move up during an open, and the MANIFEST's `next_pack` is at least every seq it used. A retry at the same prospective checkpoint position can create a chunk under a distinct digest. The abandoned chunk is absent from the retained locators. It becomes a reclaim candidate under rule 4 once a later checkpoint has passed its position, or under rule 3 after another holder takes over (§12.6);
  - a different epoch gives a different name.

  A create answered `Exists` (412) is resolved by one GET. Exactly this holder's bytes are `Created`. Any other bytes are `Corrupt(Fault{file: name, offset: 0, why: Malformed})`, refused before publication. Nothing is ever overwritten.
- **Multipart completion is not a PUT retry (Astra #18).** `complete` with `If-None-Match: *` has these outcomes:
  - a well-formed `CompleteMultipartUploadResult` is `Created`;
  - an HTTP 200 whose body is an `Error` element is that error, never success;
  - 412 is `Exists` and is resolved by the one GET above;
  - 409 (`ConditionalRequestConflict`), `NoSuchUpload`, or an `Uncertain` reply resolves as follows. A GET finds the key: exact bytes are `Created`, and other bytes are `Corrupt(.. Malformed)`. NotFound **restarts the upload with a fresh upload id and the same immutable bytes**, within the cut's remaining budget. Replaying a completion on a spent upload id is never done.

  When the budget ends, the cut is refused with `Remote(e)`. Nothing is published, AP16 loses nothing, the holder stays healthy, and the next trigger retries the cut.
- **The head's bytes differ for every (epoch, holder, position).** The residual assumption is stated as §2.1 states one for checksums: the provider's validator for two distinct head bodies is equal only with negligible probability while an old request can still arrive (Astra #17). This is a provider requirement (v2.77). The store compares tags only for equality and never reads one as a digest of the body. Q5's exact readback covers a 412. The validator assumption covers only an `Applied` reply, which is never read back.

**Frames of objects@1** (all MUST, all format 5 under §2.7 rules 1–5):

| Frame | Kind | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| CLAIM | 0x0040, 24 B | `epoch u64 ‖ holder.hi u64 ‖ holder.lo u64` (v2.43's layout, unchanged) |
| AUTHORITY | **0x00D0**, ≤ 64 KiB | `style u8` (0 virtual-hosted, 1 path-style; any other value is `Corrupt(Malformed)`), then `endpoint`, `aws_region`, `bucket` and `prefix`, each a u16 LE length and that many bytes of UTF-8. `endpoint` is 1–2,048 bytes, `aws_region` 0–64, `bucket` 3–63 and `prefix` 0–1,024. Then the **level declaration**: `count u8` (1–16), and for each level, weakest first, `name` (a u16 length and 1–64 bytes of UTF-8, unique) and `survives u8` (0 the process, 1 a host crash, 2 a holder change). On objects@1 `count` is 1 and `survives` is 2. On sim@1 (v2.73) every level but the last has `survives` 0 and the last has 2. A recorded sim@1 declaration that breaks this is `Corrupt(Malformed)`. Leftover bytes, a field outside its range, invalid UTF-8, a count of 0 or over 16, a duplicate name, or a `survives` above 2 is `Corrupt(Malformed)`. Genesis refuses a grant whose fields exceed these ranges with `Limit(Name)` before any request. It is config, never a credential. **0x0050, v2.43's AUTHORITY, is retired** (rule 5: a known kind's payload never grows). Its layout is the first five fields above, and v2.43 stores have no reader (§11.18), so a 0x0050 frame is `Unsupported(0x0050)`. |
| MARK | 0x0090, ≤ 8 KiB | `generation u64 ‖ m_epoch u64 ‖ m_digest u64 ‖ m_len u64` (the MANIFEST's name and length), `floor u64`, `depth u8` (0–3, the locator's depth), `count u32` (0–254), then `count` rows `position u64 ‖ epoch u64 ‖ digest u64 ‖ len u64`. The rows are **every earlier retained checkpoint**, one row each, the oldest included, ascending by position, all below this entry's position (§12.6). The entry itself is retained implicitly. `floor` is the smallest retained position: the first row's position, or this entry's own position when `count` is 0 (v2.48, Delta #2). A MARK is 45 + 32·count bytes, at most 8,173. |
| HEAD | 0x00A0, **136 B** | thirteen u64 LE, then 32 bytes. In order: `epoch`, `holder.hi`, `holder.lo`, `activation`, `position`, **`entry_epoch`**, `len`, `digest` (the latest entry is `e-<position>-<entry_epoch>-<digest>`, of length `len`), `c_position`, `c_epoch`, `c_len`, `c_digest` (the latest CHECKPOINT entry), `floor`, then **`binding`** (32 bytes, §12.1; named `image` before v2.55, same bytes and place). The store identity is in the HEADER. |
| LINK | 0x00B0, 24 B | `prev_epoch u64 ‖ prev_len u64 ‖ prev_digest u64`, naming the entry at position − 1. All zero at position 1. |
| LOCATE | 0x00C0, ≤ 1 MiB | rows of 32 B, at most 32,768 per frame. At depth 0 each row is `seq u64 ‖ epoch u64 ‖ len u64 ‖ digest u64`, naming a pack, ascending strictly by seq. At depth d ≥ 1 each row is `position u64 ‖ epoch u64 ‖ len u64 ‖ digest u64`, naming a depth-(d − 1) chunk object `l-<position>-<epoch>-<digest>` and its length, in seq order of the rows they hold. |

Leaf rows ascend strictly by seq across every chunk of a level, and a reader checks that order across chunk boundaries.

**HEAD rules.** These are checked on every head read, and each failure is `Corrupt(Malformed)` (Fable A3):
- `epoch ≥ 1`, `position ≥ 1`, `1 ≤ entry_epoch ≤ epoch`, `1 ≤ c_epoch ≤ epoch`, `1 ≤ floor ≤ c_position ≤ position`;
- `len` and `c_len` are at least 72 + 40 and at most `ENTRY_READ_LIMIT` (below);
- **when `position = c_position`, (`entry_epoch`, `len`, `digest`) = (`c_epoch`, `c_len`, `c_digest`)**: the latest entry *is* the checkpoint;
- the head's HEADER `epoch` equals HEAD `epoch`, and its HEADER `seq` equals `position`.

Before writing a head, a holder computes `epoch + 1` (a claim) or `position + 1` (an advance) by checked arithmetic. A claim also needs `position + 1` for its CLAIM entry, so it checks both before step 3. Reaching 2⁶³ is `Limit(Ids)` before any request (Astra #12, #13).

**What each head write sets (Astra #1, Fable L1).**
- A **claim** copies `position`, `entry_epoch`, `len`, `digest`, every `c_*`, `floor`, `activation` and `binding` unchanged, and changes only `epoch` and `holder`.
- An **advance** sets `position` to p + 1, and `entry_epoch` to its own epoch with the new entry's `len` and `digest`. It changes `c_*` and `floor` only when the entry is a CHECKPOINT, and `activation` and `binding` only for an activation CHECKPOINT (§12.7).
- A claim also copies the AUTHORITY frame **byte for byte** (Fable S2).

So the latest entry's name is always in HEAD: after any number of claims with no advance between them, the latest entry is still `e-<position>-<entry_epoch>-<digest>`.

**Chain rules** (Fable A3). Each is checked on every entry read and is `Corrupt(Malformed)` otherwise:
- a LINK's `prev_epoch` ≤ its entry's HEADER `epoch`, so epochs never fall along the chain;
- a CLAIM frame's `epoch` equals its entry's HEADER `epoch`;
- a CHECKPOINT entry's MARK rows ascend strictly and lie below its position, and its `floor` equals its first row's position, or its own position when it has no rows.

**Floor agreement (v2.48, Delta #2).** Wherever a CHECKPOINT entry is loaded from a head (recovery, a claim's recovery and rebase, a follower's start and catch-up, export, scrub), HEAD `floor` must equal that entry's MARK `floor`, and otherwise the result is `Corrupt(Malformed)`. Both come from the one capture, so the check needs no other object. **No read check looks at a predecessor checkpoint.** With `retain` 1 reclaim lawfully erases every earlier checkpoint and the entries between (§12.6), so a cold reader has only the head's own checkpoint, and an absent predecessor is never evidence of corruption. The floor's monotonicity is a property of the writer's retained-set rule (§12.6), proved by L58, not a read check. A follower that already holds its capture's MARK and loads a newer checkpoint has both in hand: a newer `floor` below its capture's is `Corrupt(Malformed)`, and nothing is fetched for that comparison.

**Entries.**
- A writer creates an entry of at most `ENTRY_LIMIT` = 72 + 40 + max(`group_bytes`, 16 + 16,777,280) bytes for its own `group_bytes`.
- A reader never needs any open's `group_bytes`. It knows each entry's `len` from its successor's LINK or from HEAD before it fetches.
- A reader refuses a `len` above `ENTRY_READ_LIMIT` = 72 + 40 + 2³² + 16 + 16,777,280 bytes before allocating (`Corrupt(Malformed)`). That is the largest `ENTRY_LIMIT` any `group_bytes` allows.
- A reader allocates exactly `len`, charged (§12.9).

| Entry | Frames after LINK | Made by |
|---|---|---|
| GROUP | 1..`group_commits` COMMIT, FORK and other journal frames, or one frame larger than `group_bytes` alone (§3.3) | an advance |
| CLAIM | one CLAIM | the first advance after a claim (§12.3) |
| CHECKPOINT | one MARK, then one LOCATE (empty at genesis) | a paused cut (AP16), and genesis |

**A CHECKPOINT entry at position c certifies the state after its own cut's operation (Q1, Astra #4, Fable F1).**
- objects@1 uses AP16's paused cut, never §3.5's concurrent one. No entry is advanced between the moment the cut reads the roots and the moment its CHECKPOINT entry is Advanced.
- The cut's **input** is the settled state through entry c − 1.
- Its MANIFEST is that state **after applying the cut's own operation**: `delete_branch` without the branch, `pin` with the pin, a cut-path `fork` with the branch, an activation's graft (§12.7), the first import's rows, or nothing for a plain `checkpoint`.
- So the state certified at c is the state after entry c. Recovery loads the checkpoint and applies the entries above c.
- The cost is stated: on objects@1 the pause includes the cut's pack uploads and its two requests, and commits wait for it. Non-blocking background uploads (commits during a cut) are deferred until measured (Q1).

**When a cut runs on objects@1.**
- It runs as today: after `checkpoint_bytes` of journal frames since the last cut, or on `checkpoint`.
- It also runs when the number of entries since the latest CHECKPOINT reaches `checkpoint_entries` (default 4096; 0 is `Missing("checkpoint_entries")` at open; Q1, Fable F10).
- An open whose recovered suffix already holds `checkpoint_entries` or more entries cuts before it returns.
- A cut refused for memory loses nothing (AP16), and the next trigger retries it.

**The objects@1 MANIFEST.** The MANIFEST bytes are AP14's, with these readings:
- `first_live` is the CHECKPOINT entry's position c;
- `prev_first` is c. objects@1 has no segments, so it names nothing, and recovery, followers and AP21 never read an earlier checkpoint through it (v2.48, Delta #2: with `retain` 1 there is no earlier retained checkpoint);
- `retired` is always the all-zero root.

Retirement on objects@1 is reclaim's (§12.6): a pack is garbage when no retained checkpoint's locator names it.

**The pack locator (Astra #2, #9, #10; v2.47 makes it a tree).** A PagePtr names a pack by `seq` only. On objects@1 a CHECKPOINT's locator maps each seq to the pack's full name and length.
- **Shape.** The CHECKPOINT entry holds one LOCATE frame, the locator's root, and MARK `depth` says what its rows name:
  - At depth 0 the rows are the pack rows themselves, at most 32,768.
  - At depth d ≥ 1 the rows name chunk objects of depth d − 1. Each chunk holds at most 32,768 rows. At every internal level, the child ranges are ordered by the pack sequences they cover. An unchanged child created at position 20 can follow a rebuilt child created at 24.
  - Depth 3 addresses 32,768⁴ = 2⁶⁰ packs, above any `next_pack` a store can reach before `Limit(Ids)`. So **every covering cut has a representable locator**, whatever `pack_bytes` and the number of live pages. The cut-size refusal of v2.46 (`Limit(Manifest)` for a locator over `ENTRY_LIMIT`) is deleted.
  - A cut builds the smallest depth that fits. It reuses, by name, every chunk whose rows are unchanged, so its cost is O(changed rows + changed chunks).
- **Coverage.** The leaf rows are exactly the packs the checkpoint's MANIFEST reaches, inherited packs of older epochs included:
  - L, every `packs` row (classes 0 and 1);
  - C, every class-2 pack that holds a page of the `packs` tree (AP21 step 0's C, since `retired` is empty).

  Leaf rows ascend strictly by seq across frames and chunks.
- **Bootstrap.** HEAD names the latest CHECKPOINT entry. Its MARK names the MANIFEST (generation, epoch, length, digest) and the locator depth. Its LOCATE frame gives the root. A cold reader needs no LIST at any step.
- **Reading, in this order, each allocation bounded and charged before its own GET (Astra #9):**
  1. the CHECKPOINT entry, of HEAD's `c_len` (≤ `ENTRY_READ_LIMIT`);
  2. the MANIFEST, of MARK's `m_len`. Before GET, refuse lengths above the current format's `MANIFEST_LIMIT` (§13.1) plus 88 bytes for HEADER and the frame envelope and 20 bytes for the optional FENCE. The pre-GET ceiling is 16,777,640 bytes in format 5. After GET, check the actual envelope and verify that the MANIFEST payload is within `MANIFEST_LIMIT`;
  3. the locator's chunks, each of the length its parent row gives, refused above 72 + 16 + 1 MiB;
  4. class-2 packs, the list-page reads of AP21 step 0. Each is one `fetch_range` of the PagePtr's 16 + `len` bytes (bounded at 8,400), then each class-2 pack is streamed once through the 65,536-byte chunk buffer with its whole-object length and digest checked against its row as the stream ends;
  5. class-0/1 packs, each refused before its GET if its row's `len` exceeds AP21 step 1's bound from that pack's `packs` row (its `frames`), then read whole.

  So no pack is read whole before the list rows that bound it are validated.
- **Checks.**
  - The set of leaf-row seqs must equal L ∪ C exactly. A missing or extra row is `Corrupt(Malformed)`. This replaces v2.46's "a row whose pack no edge reached", which assumed that every `packs` row keeps a live frame, an invariant AP16 does not state (Fable's open question).
  - A fetched pack whose length, digest, HEADER `seq` or HEADER `epoch` differs from its row is `Corrupt`.
  - A PagePtr into a seq with no row is `Dangling(stamp)`.
  - A chunk whose HEADER `seq` differs from its name's position, or whose rows break the cross-chunk order, is `Corrupt(Malformed)`.
  - These checks are AP21 steps 0–4 with "the file `p-<seq>`" read as "the object the row names".
- **Every user.** Recovery, followers, scrub, export and reclaim resolve packs through the locator of the checkpoint they work from, never by listing.

**Provider contract (Astra #8, #17, Fable F2).** objects@1 is safe only on a provider that gives all five of these, across every endpoint and client that can reach the bucket and prefix:
1. a **linearizable conditional PUT on `head`**: `If-Match: <tag>` applies only if the current head's tag is exactly `tag`, and `If-None-Match: *` applies only if no head exists. Each is evaluated against the latest applied write from any client in any region;
2. a **linearizable GET of `head`**, whose body and tag come from the same response;
3. a **validator that does not recur** for distinct bodies while an old request can still arrive, under the residual assumption stated above;
4. **create-if-absent** for entries, MANIFESTs, packs and chunks (`If-None-Match: *` on PUT and on multipart `complete`);
5. **read-after-write** by exact key for every acknowledged object, and a LIST that shows every object created before it was issued. LIST is used only by genesis's empty check, by recovery and followers as a fetch hint (§12.3), and as reclaim's candidate source. A lagging LIST only slows a fetch or leaves garbage.

The client maps **412** to `Mismatch` (for `If-Match`) and `Exists` (for `If-None-Match`). A **409** on a conditional PUT (S3's `ConditionalRequestConflict`: a conflicting request was in flight) is **retried with the same tag and body** within the budget, and is never `Mismatch` (Fable F7). Multipart completion has its own rule (above).

**Which endpoints the store accepts (v2.77).** The store never asks which company runs an endpoint. It checks the transport at every open (writer, genesis, import and follower) before any write, and the protocol at genesis. It never uses the AUTHORITY recorded in the head.
- **Transport.** The live client's endpoint must be `https`, except for the loopback simulator below. Otherwise the result is `Endpoint(Insecure)`, because the service identity is the TLS-authenticated host. Any https host is accepted: AWS (including VPC, FIPS and dual-stack hosts), Tigris, Cloudflare R2, MinIO and any other S3-compatible service.
- **Protocol, at genesis (step 5a).** After genesis or import creates entry 1 and before any head exists, it PUTs entry 1's exact bytes to entry 1's key twice: once with `If-None-Match: *`, then with `If-Match` on a tag no object carries (`"hirsel-store-condition-probe"`). Each must be refused with 412 (or the provider's 304). An `Applied` reply is `Endpoint(IgnoresIfNoneMatch)` or `Endpoint(IgnoresIfMatch)`, and any other failure is `Remote(e)`. The probe is side-effect-free: the entry is immutable, so an endpoint that ignores the condition rewrites identical bytes. A refused genesis has written no head and leaves only debris that the next genesis skips. Opening an existing store does not probe: its entries may have been reclaimed, so a correct provider could apply the create and the probe would refuse it.
- **Consistency is the operator's.** Item 1 of the provider contract below requires the conditional writes on `head` to be linearizable for the bucket as every writer and follower sees it. A probe from one client cannot show that across regions, so it is a stated requirement and not a check. It holds for single-region buckets and for buckets the provider documents as globally strongly consistent. For a multi-region bucket that is strongly consistent only within a region (for example Tigris Global and Dual-region), every writer and follower of the store must use the same region endpoint. An operator who moves a store to another endpoint must meet the requirement there.
- **`std.sim.s3`** is one map. A client reaches it in one of two ways (v2.66):
  - a client started on the in-process simulator endpoint (`start_simulated`), whose provider port belongs to the simulator;
  - the **loopback simulator** (`std.sim.s3.serve_loopback`), which other processes reach over real sockets. It serves one named bucket, path style, and answers a target outside `/<bucket>` with 404 `NoSuchBucket`. A client whose endpoint is `http://`, path style, with an IPv4 loopback literal host (`127.0.0.0/8`) is a proven client. It derives a proof key from its credential root, `HMAC-SHA256` derivation under `hirsel.sim.s3.proof`, sealed for MAC use only. It refuses every answer, error answers included, unless the answer carries `x-hirsel-sim-proof: hex(HMAC(proof key, "hirsel.sim.s3.v1\n" ‖ the request's exact Authorization value))`. The simulator proves only answers to SigV4-authenticated requests, so it is no proof oracle. The proof binds the request, not the answer: it shows that a holder of the credential root saw this request, so a process without the root cannot pass as the simulator, while the answer's status and body rest on the loopback host being the operator's own, as they do for any plain-http test endpoint. The check sends one `GetBucketLocation`. A failed or unproven answer is `Endpoint(Unproven)`.
  
  A loopback host is never accepted by its address alone: only a process that holds the credential root can answer, so another local server is refused.

**`std.object` gains** (Astra #4, #17, #18):

```hirsel
pub type Conditional = Applied(Meta) | Mismatch
pub type Precondition = Match(ETag) | Absent
pub fn store_if(mut c: Client, key: String, pre: Precondition, take body: Bytes, deadline_ns: u64) -> (Result[Conditional, Error], Bytes) waits
pub fn store_if_retry(mut c: Client, key: String, pre: Precondition, take body: Bytes, deadline_ns: u64) -> (Result[Conditional, Error], Bytes) waits
pub fn endpoint_secure(c: Client) -> bool                                     // https
pub fn bucket_location(mut c: Client, deadline_ns: u64) -> Result[String, Error] waits     // GetBucketLocation's LocationConstraint
```

`store_if` retries only three things: what cannot have been delivered (no request byte committed), 409, and 400 `RequestTimeout`. Every other outcome after delivery may have started is returned as it is: `Applied`, `Mismatch` (412), or `Uncertain(reason)` (timeout, reset after the body, 5xx, 503 `SlowDown`, 429). It never resolves by HEAD or by put id, because the store's Q5 rule (§12.3) is the only resolver. `store_no_clobber`'s resolving path stays for callers outside the authority. `complete` gains the 200-with-`Error` and `NoSuchUpload` distinctions above.

The authority uses `store_if_retry`. It resends uncertain requests within the same client attempt and deadline budget as transport retries. It returns `Applied` or `Mismatch` when either arrives, and preserves `Uncertain` on a failure after possible delivery. The authority inspects the register on `Mismatch`.

### 12.3 Claim, advance and the head poll

**The Q5 rule (one rule for every head write, genesis included).** A head write sends body B with precondition P (`Absent` at genesis, `Match(t)` otherwise):
- `Applied` → done. The new tag is the response's.
- `Uncertain` → resend exactly (B, P), within the client's retry budget and the operation's deadline. The bytes and precondition are the same, never a fresh tag.
- `Mismatch` → GET `head` once:
  - if its bytes are exactly B, the write is done, continuing from the GET's tag (an earlier send applied);
  - if they are any other bytes, **this holder's precondition is gone for good**. The current head is not P's, the head is never erased and tags never recur, so no later copy of B can apply. B **may already have applied** before the intervening write (a claim keeps the position, so the history then holds B's entry). The result is `Fenced(e)` for an advance. For a claim, the claim loop below reads the GET's bytes: another (epoch, holder) than the claim's pair (step 1) is `Lost`, and the claim's pair at another position means the incumbent advanced, so the claimant catches up privately and tries again (v2.48, v2.49). No *outstanding* ticket is acked. Whether an advance's group is in the history is decided by the next claim's head, exactly as for `Undecided`.
- If the budget or deadline runs out, or the GET itself fails, the result is `Undecided`:
  - for an advance this is sticky: the claim is dead, and the group is never acked by this open;
  - for a claim, `open` returns `Undecided` having written no entry.

**Safety.** Only this holder produces B: it holds `holder` and a position no one else writes at this epoch. Once B is the head, every later head reaches it through LINK. So "the head is B" proves B is in the history permanently, and acking on that evidence is not "retrying a failed barrier into success" (Q5, Fable F5). The Tigris probe saw exactly these outcomes for injected client timeouts (`tigris-cas-1925`):
- applied, then 412 with own bytes;
- not applied, then 200 on resend;
- an intervening writer, then 412 with other bytes.

**One owner per advance (Astra #11, Fable A3; v2.73).** The journal task owns each advance's completion, and a completion is irreversible.
- **One request at a time.** Every head request and entry create of the holder is the journal task's, sent over its `std.object.Requests`: entry creates, head writes and their Q5 resends and GETs, `fresh_snapshot` GETs and idle polls. It sends them one at a time and receives each reply before it sends the next. While a cut holds the Requests (§12.2, "When a cut runs"), the cut sends pack and MANIFEST requests and no head request, and the journal sends none. Readers' GETs (pagers, followers) use their own lanes and never request the head for the holder: a pager forwards a NotFound to the journal (§13). This holds on any lane count, so a one-lane Bucket is a valid configuration.
- **An advance is decided by its own replies.** Only the Q5 rule's replies to the advance's head write decide it. A `fresh_snapshot` GET and an idle poll run only between advances, when no head write is outstanding. They decide only the holder's pair for later work: another pair makes the holder `Fenced(e)`, and they never decide an advance.
- Once an advance is Advanced, its tickets are acked. A later `Fenced` applies to later work and never revokes that success.

**Genesis** (no head and `o.create`; Astra #4, #6, #9, #12, #20, #21, Fable L2):
1. GET `head` returns NotFound. Without `o.create` the result is `NotFound`. Run §12.1's checks for the no-head case, which refuse `o.expect = Some(_)` and `o.activation = Some(v ≠ 0)`. This all happens before any write. A racing `Lost` later can never switch an open that failed these checks onto the claim path.
2. **Empty namespace, ignoring genesis debris.** LIST the prefix page by page. A key shaped as genesis debris is skipped: `e-<1>-<1>-<digest>`, `m-<1>-<1>-<digest>`, `p-<seq>-<1>-<digest>` or `l-<1>-<1>-<digest>`, with `<1>` the zero-padded 1. Any other key is `Exists("authority")`, and nothing is written.
   - Debris is what an earlier genesis or import left when it crashed or lost before its head create. No v2.43 key has these shapes (v2.43 wrote `MANIFEST-<gen>` and `p-<seq>`).
   - A concurrent creator's debris that appears between the GET and the LIST is skipped the same way. Concurrent creators are decided in step 6.
   - Clearing a prefix that holds other keys is an operator act. There is no reader for v2.43 bytes.
3. Draw the identity and the holder (16 bytes each, `Random`).
4. Create the base: the genesis MANIFEST `m-1-1-<d>` (§3.4 step 2's fields in AP14's layout: generation 1, `next_pack` 1, `first_live` 1, `prev_first` 1, empty list roots, main at version 0, `account` 0). **A standalone import** (§12.7) instead creates its validated packs `p-<seq>-1-<d>`, any locator chunks and its MANIFEST here, all at epoch 1.
5. Create entry 1, `e-1-1-<d₁>`: HEADER(seq 1, epoch 1), LINK(0, 0, 0), MARK{generation 1, epoch 1, the MANIFEST's len and digest; floor 1; depth; no earlier retained}, and the LOCATE root (empty for a plain genesis). **The base is an ordinary CHECKPOINT.**
   5a. (v2.77) Send entry 1's bytes to its key with `If-None-Match: *`, then with `If-Match` on a tag no object carries. Both must be refused, else `Endpoint(IgnoresIfNoneMatch)` or `Endpoint(IgnoresIfMatch)` (§12.2).
6. Create `head` with `Absent`: HEAD{epoch 1, holder, activation 0, position 1, entry_epoch 1, len₁, d₁, c = (1, 1, len₁, d₁), floor 1, binding all-zero}, and the grant's AUTHORITY. Apply the Q5 rule.
   - A loser of a genesis race gets `Lost` and **returns `Lost`**. It never retries into a claim (Fable L5).
   - The loser's objects are epoch-1 debris that reclaim removes (§12.6) or a later genesis skips.
7. The first advance is the CLAIM entry at position 2 (below).

So every head names a CHECKPOINT, and HEAD has no "absent checkpoint" encoding. Recovery always starts from a MANIFEST. A crash or `Undecided` anywhere before step 6 leaves only debris, and the next `open` with `create` finishes genesis with no operator. A delayed `Absent` request of the crashed attempt can still apply. That is an ordinary genesis race, and the second opener's step 6 gets `Mismatch` then `Lost`.

**Claim** (every writer `open` of an existing store; Q4, Astra #5, #13, Fable L3, L5; v2.48 Delta #5). **A claim fences only the exact head it has already recovered and admitted.** Every step before the replace writes nothing, and a claimant that cannot serve the admitted head never deposes the incumbent:
1. **GET `head`**: its bytes and tag. **Check** the live client's transport (§12.2), once for this open; no later step repeats it. This GET's (epoch e, holder) is **the claim's pair**, fixed for the whole open (v2.49, Check #2). A rebase or catch-up changes the admitted head A, never the pair.
   - **The pair check.** Every head GET of the claim before its replace applies compares its (epoch, holder) with the claim's pair **first**: step 3's witness GET and each of its retries, and step 4's final GET and its catch-up witness GETs. Step 5's Q5 GET makes it only after the Q5 rule's exact-bytes test: its own body (epoch e + 1, this holder) is Claimed, and only other bytes are compared with the pair. The check ends when the replace applies; the CLAIM advance, the idle poll and `fresh_snapshot` follow §12.3's holder rules. A different pair returns `Lost` at once, before the GET's head is classified, before its CHECKPOINT entry is fetched and before anything is adopted from it. `Lost` outranks `Corrupt`: a missing object seen under another holder's head says nothing about the incumbent this claim recovered.
2. **Check** §12.1's opening checks on those bytes: identity, AUTHORITY, declaration, activation and binding. Also check that `epoch + 1` and `position + 1` do not reach 2⁶³ (`Limit(Ids)`). Any failure returns with nothing written.
3. **Recover and admit.** Recover read-only from that head (Recovery below, steps 1–4), with no epoch held, into private state. Then **admit** it: the private state's AP15 account is within this open's `resident_limit` (Recovery refuses as it applies), and the writer's fixed buffers (§12.9: the two entry buffers, the two head buffers and the CLAIM entry) are reserved now, before any write. The head these steps used is the **admitted head** A, with its bytes, tag and position p_A. Its (epoch, holder) is always the claim's pair. Every failure here (`Full(Allocation(c))`, `Full(Resident(c))`, `Corrupt`, `Remote`) returns with nothing written and the incumbent untouched. A NotFound during recovery takes §12.5's witness against a fresh head GET, with the pair check first: another pair is `Lost`, and nothing of that head is read or adopted. Under the claim's pair, if the object is no longer live for that head (`Reclaimed`, the incumbent's own cut and reclaim passed it), the claimant **rebases**: it discards the private state and repeats steps 2–3 from that head. A live missing object is `Corrupt(.. Absent)`. If the head's CHECKPOINT entry is itself NotFound during the witness (§12.5, "A witness lost during inspection"), the claimant takes a fresh head GET, makes the pair check again, and decides again; a witness still undecided when `claim_ms` ends returns `Lost` with nothing written, like every other attempt the loop's deadline ends.
4. **The final GET.** GET `head`:
   - another (epoch, holder) than the claim's pair: the store has another holder, and the result is `Lost`;
   - exactly A's bytes: go to step 5 at once with this GET's tag t;
   - the claim's pair at another position p: the incumbent advanced. **Nothing is written.** The claimant rechecks step 2's byte checks on the new bytes (no provider request), **catches up privately** to the new head and admits again (step 3's admission, against the grown state), and the caught-up head becomes A. Then it repeats step 4. Catching up applies entries p_A + 1..p by Recovery's walk from p down to p_A + 1, whose LINK must reach A's entry at p_A, when the new head's `c_position` ≤ p_A. When the new head names a later checkpoint (`c_position` > p_A), the entries between may be lawfully reclaimed (`retain` 1), so the claimant **rebases**: it discards the private state and recovers from the new head's checkpoint. A NotFound during catch-up takes step 3's witness on a fresh head GET, pair check first: another pair is `Lost`, and under the claim's pair a `Reclaimed` verdict is a rebase on that head. A refusal during catch-up or rebase (`Full` because the incumbent grew past this claimant's `resident_limit`, `Corrupt`, `Remote`) returns that error with nothing written: the incumbent keeps serving.
5. **The Q4 pair.** **At once replace the head** with `Match(t)` and HEAD{epoch e + 1, this holder, every other field copied from A (§12.2)}. Nothing runs between the final GET and the replace, so the replace is one round trip after its GET and beats a saturated holder (Q4). Apply the Q5 rule:
   - `Applied`, or a 412 whose GET shows this body: claimed at e + 1. The old holder's next head write gets `Mismatch`, then `Fenced`.
   - a 412 whose GET shows the claim's pair at another position: the incumbent advanced between the final GET and the replace, and nothing was fenced. Back off (the claim loop below), catch up privately from that GET's bytes as step 4 does, and repeat step 4.
   - a 412 whose GET shows another (epoch, holder) than the claim's pair: `Lost`.
   - `Undecided`: `open` returns `Undecided` having written no entry.
6. **Serve the admitted head.** The claimant's private state *is* the state at A's position, so no history is applied after the fence. **The first advance is the CLAIM entry** at p_A + 1, {e + 1, holder}, through the ordinary advance path in the buffers step 3 reserved. `open` returns once it is Advanced, so a returned Db has its claim recorded in the history.
   - If this advance is `Fenced`, a later claimant replaced the head after step 5, and `open` returns `Lost`. A claim that wins step 5 but returns no Db is counted in L52 as a fence, not as a successful open (Astra #13).
   - A crash between steps 5 and 6 leaves a head of epoch e + 1 over an entry of a lower epoch, which the `entry_epoch` rule allows.
   - The open-time cut (§12.2, "When a cut runs") follows the CLAIM advance. A refused cut does not fail the open: it loses nothing (AP16), the Db is returned, and the next trigger retries it.

**The residual (stated).** After a won replace, only the CLAIM advance can fail: a claimant crash, or `Remote` or `Undecided` on its entry or head write. That leaves a head of epoch e + 1 that no open holds, and the next open claims e + 2. No memory admission, recovery or catch-up runs after the fence, so a healthy incumbent is never deposed by a claimant that turns out unable to serve it (v2.48 replaces v2.47's step 5 and its residual for the delta's growth).

**The claim loop (Q4, Fable F4, L5, Astra #13).** A claim attempt ends in one of three ways besides success:
- **The incumbent advanced** (step 4 saw a moved head, or step 5's Q5 GET showed the claim's pair at another position). The incumbent is the claim's pair, and only its own advances, cuts and reclaims are caught up or rebased over. The claimant catches up privately and repeats step 4. After a step-5 `Mismatch` it first backs off with jitter from `Random` (base 10 ms, doubling, at most 1 s); a moved head at step 4 wrote nothing and repeats at once.
- **The pair changed**: a head GET before the replace applied (final, witness, or a Q5 GET that is not this claimant's own body) shows another pair than step 1's, so another claimant won, and `open` returns `Lost` at once. It never adopts that claimant's head, never rebases onto it, and never deposes a fresh claimant mid-recovery (v2.49). The launcher decides whether to try again.
- **A refusal** (validation, `Full`, `Corrupt`, `Remote`, `Undecided`): returned as it is, never retried.

Every request, catch-up, rebase and backoff is bounded by the time left of `o.claim_ms` (default 30,000; 0 means one attempt) on the local monotonic clock. When it ends, `open` returns `Lost` with nothing written by the attempt in progress.

Progress is conditional, and stated as such. An attempt succeeds when its replace reaches the register before the incumbent's next head write. A holder that writes its head continuously can starve a claimant for the whole `claim_ms`, and then keeps serving. The remedy is the launcher's: stop the incumbent (RUNNER-SPEC item 5's generation fence). The loop only absorbs a lost race.

**Recovery** (objects@1, replacing §3.4 steps 1–5; Fable L4):
1. From HEAD take `c` and `p`. Allocate the chain list, 24 bytes × (p − c), charged (§12.9). An allocator refusal is `Full(Allocation(c))` before any GET.
2. **Name the suffix.** The head names entry p as `e-<p>-<entry_epoch>-<digest>`.
   - As a **fetch hint only**, LIST `e-` keys after `e-<c>` in pages, and `fetch_range` bytes 0..112 (HEADER and LINK) of each listed name on parallel lanes.
   - Then walk down from p to c + 1 by LINK, using each successor's LINK to name its predecessor. Read the prefix of any name the hint lacked serially.
   - A listed name that the walk does not reach is ignored. A missing or extra listed name changes only speed. Only the chain from the head is applied.
   - Record (epoch, len, digest) per position. The LINK at position c + 1 must name the checkpoint (c, c_epoch, c_len, c_digest) that HEAD names. Otherwise the result is `Corrupt(Malformed)`: a CHECKPOINT shortcut outside the chain is refused.
3. **Load the checkpoint** in the order "Reading" gives (§12.2), then run AP21 steps 0–5 over it.
4. **Apply** entries c + 1..p in position order. Each is fetched whole, with exactly its recorded `len`, and its digest, HEADER and frames are checked before apply. GROUP frames apply exactly as §3.4 step 6. CLAIM frames change no state. A CHECKPOINT entry above c cannot occur (`Corrupt(Malformed)`), because HEAD names the latest. Fetches may run ahead on parallel lanes, bounded by the per-lane buffer (§12.9).
5. **Account** as §3.4 step 7. There is no rotation: the next entry is p + 1.

**Advance** (the journal task, one group, replacing §3.3's write and sync for objects@1):
1. Create the entry at p + 1: LINK to entry p, then the group's frames. The entry write is not a commit point. `Uncertain` and `Exists` resolve as create-only says, and an unresolved failure is `Remote(e)`, sticky poison with nothing acked.
2. Replace the head with `Match(own last tag)` and the fields §12.2 gives for an advance. Apply the Q5 rule.

| Q5 outcome of the head write | Result | The store |
|---|---|---|
| `Applied`, or `Mismatch` with own bytes | Advanced(p + 1) | acks the group's tickets at every declared level reached (§12.4) |
| `Mismatch` with other bytes | Fenced(e) | sticky. Health becomes `Fenced(e)` (§12.3, "Health"). The Db accepts only `close`, and every outstanding ticket is `Fenced(e)` |
| failed before any byte of the head write was delivered, after the budget | Refused | sticky poison, `Remote(e)` (§3.8) |
| budget or deadline exhausted after possible delivery, or the resolving GET failed | Undecided | sticky poison, `Undecided`. The claim is dead, and the group's tickets are never acked by this open |

At most one head write is outstanding, and entry p + 2 is created only after p + 1's head write is decided (v2.73). Creating p + 2 during that write is deferred until a measurement asks for it. With that change, p + 2's LINK would name p + 1, and p + 2 would be an orphan if p + 1 ended Fenced or Undecided.

**Tickets after the open ends (Astra #11).**
- A ticket for which `durable_at(t, L)` returned `Ok` keeps returning `Ok` at L and at every weaker level, after Fenced or Undecided too. Its commit is in D[L] for good.
- An **outstanding** ticket (not yet acked at the level asked) of an Undecided or Fenced open is terminal (`Undecided` or `Fenced(e)`) at that level and every stronger one. A ticket acked only at a weaker level is outstanding at the stronger ones.
- Every ticket is `Foreign` to any other open (§1.6).
- Whether an outstanding ticket's commit is in the history is decided by the next successful claim's head alone. Its ticket was never acked, so either answer is correct.
- A client that must not duplicate an effect after an unknown outcome uses its stream position (§1.8) or its own idempotency key. The store gives no per-transaction receipt beyond the call record's life (Astra #18).

**The idle head poll (Q3).** While the holder is healthy and no head write is outstanding, the journal task GETs `head` with `If-None-Match: <own last tag>` once every `o.head_poll_ms` (default 1,000; 0 is `Missing("head_poll_ms")` at open) on the local monotonic clock:
- 304, or 200 with this holder's own (epoch, holder), changes nothing;
- 200 with another (epoch, holder) makes the holder `Fenced(e)`, sticky, and publishes it as health;
- a failed poll changes nothing and is retried at the next tick. It is a read, so it never poisons. Health counts consecutive failed polls, so an operator can see a partitioned holder.

The poll runs only while the Db is open: a runner that unloads the place (`idle_ms`, RUNNER §14.4) closes it, and the poll stops. It does not run during a cut's uploads, because a head write is then imminent and decides the same question.

**Health (Astra #14, Fable L6).**

```hirsel
pub type Health = Ok(u32) | Fenced(u64) | Undecided | Poisoned(IoError) | Remote(std.object.Error)   // Ok carries consecutive failed polls
pub fn health(db: Db) -> Health                                              // the current value
pub fn on_unhealthy[M: send](mut db: Db, take to: Sender[M], take m: M) -> Result[(), Error]   // sends m once, when health leaves Ok
```

The poll, the Q5 rule and poison set it, and it never returns to `Ok` within an open. `on_unhealthy` registers one message, which the journal task sends on `to` when health first leaves `Ok` (at once if it already has). Delivery is an ordinary channel send into the caller's own inbox, as `clock.alarm` delivers, so an idle receiver wakes on it with no new task primitive. A full or closed channel is the receiver's: the health value stays set and every later store call returns the error. RUNNER-SPEC v2.34 registers the head's inbox and ends the run abnormally on that message (RUNNER §2.1 "Poison and fence"). The value-returning `healthy` of v2.46's text is `health`.

**Local reads.** Plain `snapshot(db)` and every query stay local reads at V, with no authority request: RAM for Memory collections, and for Tiered ones (§13) the cache or an immutable pack GET, never `head`. So a partitioned, unkilled holder serves reads of its own durable or visible state until its next head write or poll reaches the bucket. Under a working path to the bucket, and given a serviced timer, a free lane and a completing request, that lasts at most `head_poll_ms` plus one request's deadline. The bound is liveness, not safety. A client that needs current state uses `fresh` or `fresh_snapshot`. The poll costs one conditional GET per interval per idle holder, nothing while groups flow (an advance confirms the head), and one lane and the head buffer (§12.9).

**Holder change.** A claim keeps every commit for which `durable_at(L)` returned, for every level L whose declared `survives` is 2. On objects@1 that is its one level (§12.4).

### 12.4 Levels (Q2)

| Provider | Levels, weakest first | `survives` | Survives holder change |
|---|---|---|---|
| memory@1 | `memory` | 0 | no |
| log@1 | `host` (`process` later, §12.2) | 1 | a same-host reopen only, which is log@1's only holder change |
| objects@1 | the one name the grant gives | 2 | yes |
| sim@1 | the grant's `SimLevels`: its weak names, then `strongest` | 0 for each weak level, 2 for the strongest | the strongest only |

- **A level is the authority's declaration.** The store does not verify what a bucket replicates. It does fix the declaration: AUTHORITY records the ordered (name, survives) list at genesis, on sim@1 as on objects@1. Every open compares the grant's list with it exactly before claiming, and a difference is `Declared(name)` (Astra #13). Removing, renaming, reordering or weakening a level is an incompatible declaration, never a silent remap.
- D[L] is a prefix of the commit order. For L weaker than L′, D[L′] ⊆ D[L] ⊆ V.
- `durable_at(t, L)` returns once t's commit, and every commit before it on any branch, is in D[L]. Each level has its own waiter list, woken when D at that level grows: by its own barrier, or by a stronger level's (sim@1, below). An idle last group therefore wakes a stronger waiter when its stronger barrier completes, and a weaker level's progress never wakes a stronger waiter. `durable` is `durable_at` at the strongest level.
- A `Level` is bound to its StoreId and, by name, to the declaration it was resolved under. Another store's Level is `Foreign`. It has no equality and no order. Levels cross the wire only as names.
- **The runner's release gate is the strongest level** (Q2). The strongest level of every authority M2 builds survives every holder change that authority supports. Replies, subscription batches, outgoing calls, wakes and portable `Position`s wait for `durable`. There is **no `release_level`** and no weaker runner release. A weaker release needs a real multi-level authority and an epoch-tagged `Position` / `BaseLost` protocol, which are later work. `durable_at` at a weaker level remains for explicit callers, and what they do with the answer is theirs.

**sim@1 with several levels (Astra #12, Fable A4; v2.73).** sim@1 is the objects@1 protocol, unchanged, plus one barrier per weak level, owned by the grant's `LevelWorld` (§12.1):
- **The register is the strongest level.** It is the law's `std.sim.s3` service. The head write is the strongest level's barrier, Advanced means it applied, and the strongest level declares `survives` 2. The register (fence, epoch, the strongest frontier) survives every holder change and crash the law makes.
- **A weak level advances on its own barrier.** After each entry create at position p, the journal task puts (p, the entry's last frame seq) in its `LevelSync`. This is a latest-value cell, so the journal never waits on it. For each weak level L the world logs `Requested(p)` at L. Unless a `LevelHold` holds L, it then completes L-sync(p), logs `Synced(p)` at L, and sends the open's journal task `WeakSynced(L, seq)`, which wakes waiters through the per-level lists. A weak barrier never moves the head and writes no object.
- **D[L] is the larger of L's own synced frontier and D at every stronger level.** So an applied head write also advances every weak level, and a stronger level's progress wakes waiters at a weaker one. A weaker level's progress never wakes a stronger waiter.
- **Weak state belongs to the process.** Each weak level declares `survives` 0. A crash or a dropped Db loses its frontier, and the next open, which always claims, starts it at the claimed head. A weak level never declares 2: a holder change keeps exactly the head chain, and "the head is B" is Q5's only commit evidence (§12.3), so a weak level that survived would be a second commit point beside the register. Nor does it declare 1: every sim@1 writer open claims, so no event keeps a holder's state across its own crash. `SimLevels` has no field for either, and §12.2 refuses a recorded one.
- **Readers see the strongest prefix.** `fresh`, `fresh_snapshot`, followers and `at_least` read the head, so they target D[strongest]. A held-back strongest barrier with a weaker level ahead makes a fresh follower answer the strongest prefix: with D[durable] = 6 and D[volatile] = 7, the answer is 6. A law holds the strongest barrier with a `std.sim.s3` hold on the head PUT (§12.10, "Owed cases", S0).
- After a crash of the holder with weak state ahead, the next holder claims from the register. That is the strongest prefix plus, if a head write was outstanding, whatever the register applied. The weak tail of the crashed holder is gone.
- **Charges.** The `LevelSync` cell, the open's `WeakSynced` handling and one waiter list per declared level are charged to the opener at open, beside §12.9's fixed buffers. `sizes.hirsel` gives the exact figure. The `LevelWorld`'s task and log are charged to the law that made it, through `bytes`.

L55 and L56 run on sim@1.

### 12.5 Followers and fresh reads

```hirsel
pub opaque type Follower                                                     // not send: holds the objects@1 Client's task-affine Workers (v2.69 B)
pub opaque type Followers
pub fn followers() -> Followers
pub opaque type FollowerService                                              // v2.69 B: not send; holds the provisioning task's Task handle
pub fn follower_service(tasks: Tasks, bytes: u64) -> Result[FollowerService, Error] waits   // start outside every step bound (below)
pub fn close_follower_service(take s: FollowerService) -> Result[(), Error] waits
pub opaque type FollowerOwner: send                                          // a request endpoint of one service
pub fn follower_owner(s: FollowerService) -> Result[FollowerOwner, Error]
pub opaque type FollowerSlot: send                                           // the sole command endpoint of one provisioned apply worker
pub fn follower_slot(owner: FollowerOwner, p: FollowerPlan) -> Result[FollowerSlot, Error] waits
pub fn follower(mut source: Followers, take slot: FollowerSlot, take a: Authority, c: Clock, expect: Option[StoreId]) -> Result[Follower, Error] waits   // v2.69 B: replaces (tasks, a, c, o)
// v2.57: follower_table and follower_index are deleted; `declare_follower(f)` binds handles in mode Follower (§1.2)
pub fn follower_floor(mut f: Follower, at_most: u64) -> Result[Option[Snapshot], Error] waits   // v2.57 (M2): the newest retained checkpoint at or below a version, for a projector's base (§1.14)
pub fn follower_branch(f: Follower, name: String) -> Option[Branch]
pub fn applied(f: Follower, b: Branch) -> Result[Position, Error]
pub fn catch_up(mut f: Follower, deadline_ns: u64) -> Result[Position, Error] waits   // main's applied Position
pub fn at_least(mut f: Follower, p: Position, deadline_ns: u64) -> Result[Snapshot, Error] waits
pub fn fresh(mut f: Follower, deadline_ns: u64) -> Result[Snapshot, Error] waits
pub fn snapshot_follower(f: Follower, b: Branch) -> Result[Snapshot, Error]          // Gone(id) for a deleted branch, Unseen(id) before creation, Foreign for another store
pub fn fresh_snapshot(mut db: Db, deadline_ns: u64) -> Result[Snapshot, Error] waits   // the holder's fresh read
pub type Position { store: StoreId, branch: u32, version: u64 }
pub fn position(mut db: Db, t: Ticket) -> Result[Position, Error] waits
pub type Claim { epoch: u64, holder: Bytes }                                         // holder: the head's 16 bytes
pub type HeadView { store: StoreId, activation: u64, binding: Digest, claim: Claim }
pub fn follower_head(f: Follower) -> Result[HeadView, Error]                         // the head the published state was loaded from
pub fn claim_of(db: Db) -> Result[Claim, Error]                                      // this open's pair (objects@1, sim@1)
```

- **Binding (Astra #15, #19; v2.57).** `declare_follower(f)` binds tables and indexes over the follower's applied catalog in mode `Follower`, with `Open`'s checks (`Missing`, `Schema`, `Changed`, `Undeclared`, §1.2), and `follower_branch` binds a branch. They never create. The follower's registry has no extractors: its handles read only.
  - A value schema that the stored list does not hold is `Missing("schema")`. A follower never appends.
  - `follower_floor(f, v)` returns the newest CHECKPOINT the follower can still read at or below version v of main, as a Snapshot, or None when none is retained; it is built with M2's reclaim floor (§12.6).
  - The handles carry the StoreId and work with the follower's Snapshots, so `get`, `scan`, `find`, `look` and the pages work unchanged. A follower-only process needs no Db.
- **The apply worker (v2.69 B, MEM-30; astra mem30-apply-grant-2043 rank 1).**
  - **Provisioning.** `follower_service(tasks, bytes)` spawns the provisioning task with root limit `bytes`. The caller starts it from `main` or a task with no step bound current, before entering bounded work: a step bound cannot be named (MEM-30), so this is the caller's contract, as for `open`'s tasks, and a service started under a bound copies that bound once into a task that never gets more. A standalone follower process starts its own in its startup. `follower_owner(s)` makes a request endpoint, charged to its caller. `follower_slot(owner, p)` may be called inside a bound: it asks the service, which admits Q and then spawns the worker with root limit N (§1.1) against its own limit, outside every bound, and keeps the worker's Task handle until retirement. A refusal is `Full(Allocation(c))` at the admission that failed, with `c` the service limit's room, and any part of Q already admitted is released. A slot request abandoned after admission closes the undelivered endpoint and retires the worker.
  - **The starter's charges (v2.70, D2).** The **starter** is the task that calls `follower_service` and then, on that service, `follower_owner`, `follower_slot`, `follower` and the follower's requests. Outside `bytes` its limit is charged exactly `follower_starter_bytes()` = 288 + max(I, P, K) at its peak, with every term at its MEM-24 logical size:
    - **The service task: 288**, which is 256 + 0 (its result is `()`) + 32, held until `close_follower_service` (or the service's drop) joins it.
    - **The owner endpoint: 0.** `follower_owner` adds a sender to the service's request channel, which is inside `bytes`, and `channel.sender` admits nothing (CONC-4).
    - **One transient at a time**, the largest of three:
      - I, the startup reply: one capacity-one channel of `Result[FollowerOwner, Error]` that carries the first owner out of the starting service;
      - P, a slot request: the boxed request (its plan copy and reply `Sender`) and one capacity-one channel of `Result[FollowerSlot, Error]`;
      - K, a follower request (`follower`'s bind, `catch_up`, `follower_floor`, `at_least`, `fresh`): the boxed request payload and one capacity-one channel of `Result[response, Error]`.
    - **What makes it exact.** A `FollowerPlan` holds no heap storage (§1.1), so the plan copy inside P allocates nothing. The service and the worker free a request's box before they reply, and drop the reply `Sender` right after sending. The requester takes the reply, then waits on the same receiver until it returns `Closed`, and only then returns. So a call's transient is refunded before the call returns, and at most one is live on the starter. The calls are sequential on the starter, because `FollowerService` and `Follower` are not `send` and one `Follower` makes one request at a time.
    - **Everything else is someone else's.** The service's request channel, its loop state and each slot's Q are inside `bytes`. A worker's allocations draw on its N. A reply's payload (a capture, a Snapshot, an error's String) keeps the record of the payer that admitted it (MEM-20), so it is never the starter's even after it reaches the starter. The `Followers` source is a plain counter value and allocates nothing.
    - **Derived, not copied (v2.76).** Store computes I, P, K, Q, S and the worker's 288 + N in functions from the types they price, `charge.channel(bytes[Result[FollowerOwner, Error]], 1)`, `charge.boxed(bytes[Provision])` and so on (MEM-33). The `FOLLOWER_*` constants are deleted. The figures below are a hand derivation, which Store's L85 checks against those functions, and no other package states them.
    - **Logical sizes of the built types.** `Error` is 56: 8 plus its largest payloads, `Corrupt(Fault)` = 24 + 8 + 16 and `Remote(std.object.Error)` = 8 + 8 + 32, each 48. Then:
      - I = 64 + (8 + max(24, 56)) = **128**.
      - P: the provision box is round8(330 + 24) = 360, where the plan is 330 = `Kind` 24 + `Options` 290 + 8 + 8. The reply channel is 64 + 8 + 378 = 450, where the slot is 378 = 330 + 24 + 24. So P = **810**.
      - K uses a payload box of round8(8 + 242 + 24 + 8) = 288. The transport is 8 + 234 for `std.object.Requests`. The reply channel is 64 + 8 + 304 = 376. Its widest response carries a 16-byte optional capture, a 236-byte Snapshot and a 36-byte optional Position, plus two 8-byte tags. The Snapshot has three 16-byte optional paging inventories. So K = **664**.
      - The figure is 288 + 810 = **1,098**. L85 measures each request's box and reply channel charges and checks them against the corresponding constant.
  - **Binding.** A slot moves once into `follower`. A Directory plan serves log@1 and a Bucket plan objects@1 with its lane configuration; another authority is `Missing("follower_kind")` before recovery. On objects@1 the open splits the Client: the Follower keeps the task-affine Workers and the worker gets only the sendable `Requests` endpoint. On log@1 the worker reads the directory under the writer exclusion and sync rules below. A failed `follower` publishes no handle, draws no follower number and retires its worker; no worker stays attached to a failed open, and reopening needs a fresh slot.
  - **What runs where.** Recovery for the first capture, `catch_up`, `follower_floor` and the apply of `at_least` and `fresh` run on the worker: validation, the branch searches those jobs need, log and object recovery and private replay. The caller takes the steps of its own request, wait and result handling; a suspended wait takes none. `at_least`'s deadline and polling, and a query body on a Snapshot, take steps on the task running them.
  - **One publication point.** The worker serializes requests. Each request names the caller's published capture and carries its own single-use reply endpoint. The worker prepares a complete candidate and the result the caller needs, and never publishes. The live call checks its deadline and that the candidate applies to its published capture, then publishes by **one non-waiting, infallible swap** of the handle's capture: roots, applied position, watermark, head metadata and stamp domain together. `follower_floor` returns an optional historical Snapshot and leaves the capture in place. A call that fails, expires or is abandoned before the swap leaves the prior capture authoritative; a cancellation observed after the swap keeps it. §13.5 still governs eviction of a Cold capture.
  - **Cancellation.** Before the worker accepts a request, the caller's unwind drops what it owns. After acceptance the worker owns the request and its scratch through cleanup. A closed reply endpoint or a discarded queued reply drops the candidate, and a surviving follower sends a new request from its actual capture. The worker's receiver never holds a sender to its own queue, so a late reply can never become another request's result.
  - **Retirement.** Dropping the Follower closes its command endpoint; the worker drains or abandons its job, ends, and the service joins it under CONC-6/8 and frees its entry. A provider operation still running keeps its backing until it completes or aborts. Closing the service retires every unclaimed slot. A request whose worker or service is gone returns `Retired` (v2.71). Every failure of an apply keeps its own value, including `Io(Closed)` if a provider reported `Closed` (§12.9).
- **Starting and catching up.** `follower` runs recovery's steps 1–4 (§12.3) without claiming, on its worker. `catch_up` runs them again from its applied position up to a freshly read head.
  - Each run **builds the next state privately and publishes roots and applied position together**. A catch-up that fails, for any reason, leaves the previous published state and its Snapshots intact, so `applied` never moves backwards (Astra #17).
  - A follower takes no lock, writes nothing, never runs a body and never claims. Only the chain from the head is followed, so an orphan entry, a losing claim's write or a fenced holder's write is never applied.
  - While a catch-up runs, both the published state and the private one are charged to the follower's `resident_limit` (Astra #9). A refusal is `Full(Resident(c))`, and the published state stays.
- **Work and charges (MEM-30, Fable F14; v2.69 B).** Applying runs on the follower's provisioned worker under its grant N (§12.9). A caller of `catch_up`, `at_least` or `fresh` takes the steps of its own call and wait only, never the apply work for another client's lag, and its request never spawns, never copies or debits its fuel and never moves a byte charge between payers.
- **Position (Astra #14, #23).** `Position` is `{store, branch id, version}`. Branch ids are never reused (`next_branch` only rises), and a version on a branch is the same on every machine.
  - **Domain.** `position(db, t)` is defined for a ticket of a commit. **A `Journal` ticket carries its commit's branch and version** (§1.6, `Mark = Journal(seq, branch, version)`), so the Db keeps no table of issued tickets. It waits `durable(t)` (the strongest level, Q2), then returns them. A saved ticket answers after any number of cuts.
  - For a `Cut` ticket (`checkpoint`, `pin`, `delete_branch`), `position` returns `Missing("position")`: those operations make no branch version to name. A reader that must observe a pin uses the pin.
  - A Position of another store is `Foreign`.
  - `at_least(f, p)` applies until branch `p.branch` holds a version ≥ `p.version`, and returns that branch's Snapshot. The deadline and branch cases go as follows:
    - If the applied catalog has `next_branch > p.branch` and no branch `p.branch`, the branch was deleted or adopted, and the result is `Gone(p.branch)`.
    - At the deadline with the branch applied, the result is `Behind(applied(f, branch))`, never an older Snapshot.
    - At the deadline with `next_branch ≤ p.branch`, the follower has not yet seen the branch's creation, and the result is `Unseen(p.branch)`.
  - **Read-your-writes** means the snapshot observes a prefix of the history that contains the write. Later commits may have overwritten or deleted the row, with their usual meaning.
- **What a follower shows.** Only entries the head names, so only D[strongest].
- **The head of a capture (v2.49, Check #1).** `follower_head(f)` returns the store identity, HEAD `activation`, HEAD `binding` and the (epoch, holder) of the head that the published state was loaded from. It is published with the roots and applied position, so it and every `snapshot_follower` taken before the next `catch_up` describe **one capture**: the activation, binding and pair are the head's, and the rows are the state at that head. A follower opened with `expect = Some(id)` makes §12.1's identity check (`Foreign`, and `NotFound` with no head); a follower makes none of the activation, binding or declaration checks, which select a writer. `claim_of(db)` returns a holder's own pair, fixed for its open (§12.3). log@1 has no HEAD and no pair, so on a log@1 follower or Db both are `Missing("head")`.
- **Fresh (Astra #5, #11, Fable F9).**
  - On objects@1, `fresh`, `fresh_snapshot` and the idle poll send `If-None-Match` with the last observed tag. A 304 keeps the cached HEAD. A 200 goes through normal HEAD validation, even if the provider always returns a body. The tag lives only in memory and is outside the store and release identities.
  - `fresh(f)` reads the head once and catches up to it. It shows every commit whose Advanced was applied to the register before the call began, because such a head write precedes the GET in the register's linear order.
  - `fresh_snapshot(db)` on the holder (v2.73):
    - It first drains `durable`. Every outstanding head write ends in Advanced, Fenced or Undecided by its own Q5 replies, each within its own budget. A drain that ends Fenced or Undecided returns that error.
    - The journal task then makes one head GET between advances (§12.3, "One owner per advance"). `deadline_ns` bounds that GET only. It compares **(epoch, holder)**, never the tag. Another pair is `Fenced(e)`, sticky. A failed GET or the deadline is `Remote(e)` and changes no health, because it is a read.
    - During a cut, the request waits in the journal's inbox until the cut hands the Requests back.
    - It returns a Snapshot at the holder's **durable** version, the last Advanced group. Because the caller holds `mut db` and no commit is made during the call, that is also V. It never shows a commit that an Undecided group could take back.

    The holder keeps the roots of its last durable version for this and for subscription batches.
  - Either costs one head GET, plus the entry GETs a follower lacks. There are no leases.
- **A missing object (Astra #8, #17, Fable A2, F12).** A follower works from one **capture**: the CHECKPOINT c_f its published state was loaded from, and the chain from c_f to its applied head. On NotFound for a named object:
  - **An entry at position q.** GET `head`. If q < the head's `floor`, the result is `Reclaimed(floor)`. Otherwise the entry is on the chain (every head ever applied is a prefix of every later chain, because a claim keeps the position), so it is live, and the result is `Corrupt(Fault{file: name, offset: 0, why: Absent})`.
  - **A MANIFEST, pack or chunk named by c_f.** GET `head`, then its CHECKPOINT entry. If c_f's (position, epoch, digest) is that checkpoint or a row of its MARK, c_f is still retained, so everything c_f names is live, and the result is `Corrupt(.. Absent)`. Otherwise c_f has left the retained set, and the result is `Reclaimed(floor)`. The capture's eviction is the reason, whatever any other checkpoint names.
  - **A witness lost during inspection.** If the head's CHECKPOINT entry is itself NotFound (a newer cut and reclaim raced the witness), take a fresh head GET and decide again. This repeats until the caller's deadline, then the result is `Behind(applied)` with the old state still published.
  - The previous published state stays readable in every case. `catch_up` after `Reclaimed` restarts from the new head's checkpoint.
